feedback.correct: Great. You connected the leaders’ fear for their power with the changes Islam brought.
feedback.incorrect: The first paragraph gives the leaders’ view of Islam, the second explains their respect, and the last paragraph is about usury, zakat and sadaqah.

languageFocusExercises.title: How Many Is “Almost None”?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 12. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: “In the first few years of the call to Islam, almost none of Mecca’s super-rich people became Muslims.” This means that not one super-rich person in Mecca became a Muslim in those years.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Almost none” means “very, very few”, not “zero”. The writer chooses a careful quantity word so the claim is not stronger than the evidence. “In the first few years” also limits the claim to one period. Accurate history writing often depends on small words like these.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Almost none” leaves room for a very small number.
feedback.incorrect: Compare “none” and “almost none”. What does “almost” add to the meaning?

languageFocusExercises.title: Priorities and Reported Feelings
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence so that it keeps the same meaning. Use the start that is given.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you express a priority in another way and turn a reported feeling into a reason?

transformItems.source: Keeping their power and unity was very important for them.
transformItems.frame: It was very important for them [blank].
answers: to keep their power and unity
to keep their unity and power

transformItems.source: The leaders of Quraysh felt that Islam was a danger to their power and did not accept it.
transformItems.frame: The leaders of Quraysh did not accept Islam [blank] a danger to their power.
answers: because they felt that it was
because they felt that Islam was
as they felt that it was
since they felt that it was
because they thought that it was

languageFocusExercises.explanation: An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence (“Keeping their power … was very important”); “It was important + to + verb” says the same thing. Starting with “Keeping …” puts the leaders’ priority at the front. “Felt that …” reports the leaders’ own view of Islam: The writer shows this was how they saw it, and the “because” clause makes it the reason for their refusal.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the priority and the reported view in new sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use “to + verb” after “for them”. Item 2: start with “because they felt …”. Check the first two paragraphs of Chapter 12.

languageFocusExercises.title: Status, Rules and Pressure
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 12 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases tell us about the leaders’ status and the changes Islam brought?

matchingPairs.right: Others respected and admired them a lot.
the people who looked after visitors to the holy place

matchingPairs.left: turned the people against the new religion
matchingPairs.right: made others hostile to Islam
the Qur’an said that people must not do it

matchingPairs.left: Islam also commanded zakat and sadaqah
matchingPairs.right: Islam made giving to those in need a duty

correctAnswer.They had high prestige: Others respected and admired them a lot.
correctAnswer.caretakers of pilgrimage: the people who looked after visitors to the holy place
correctAnswer.the Qur’an forbade this: the Qur’an said that people must not do it
correctAnswer.Islam also commanded zakat and sadaqah: Islam made giving to those in need a duty

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Forbid” (past: forbade) means “say that something must not be done”; “command” means “order as a duty”. “Turn someone against something” means “make them hostile to it”. “Prestige” is the respect a person or group has in society. These words show both why the leaders had power and how Islam challenged it.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each phrase with its meaning in the chapter.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 12 again. Replace each phrase with your answer and check that the sentence still makes sense.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain Resistance to Change
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say six sentences about a group that did not want a change.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why did the group not want the change?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong answer should include a quantity expression, a reported viewpoint with “felt/thought that”, a reason with “because/because of”, an -ing clause as subject to express a priority, a contrast with “but”, and a purpose phrase with “to + verb”.

feedback.correct: Keep the six sentences connected so the reader can follow the group’s position, priority, contrast and purpose.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Use “almost all / almost none / only a few” to describe a group.
discussionPrompts.example: In the first weeks of the new phone rule, almost none of the older students agreed with it.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Report a viewpoint with “felt/thought that...”.
discussionPrompts.example: They felt that the rule was unfair to them.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give a reason with “because” or “because of”.
discussionPrompts.example: They were angry because they used their phones to talk to their friends at break.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Use an -ing form as the subject: “Keeping/Protecting/Changing ... was important.”
discussionPrompts.example: Keeping their freedom was very important for them.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — Contrast an old practice with a new rule using “but”.
discussionPrompts.example: Before, students could use their phones at any time, but the new rule allowed them only after school.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 6 — Explain the purpose of the new rule with “to + verb”.
discussionPrompts.example: The school made this rule to help students focus in class and talk to each other more.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What was very important for the Quraysh leaders?
beforeYouRead.quote: Keeping their power and unity was very important for them.

iCan: I can explain why the leaders of Quraysh were against Islam.
I can say what people felt and what was important to them.
I can explain why some people resist a new rule.

pages.title: Opposition to Islam
pages.content:
At first, the leaders of Mecca only mocked Islam. Whenever Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) walked by, they laughed and said that he was talking about messages from heaven. But when the Qur’an criticized the idols and warned against false worship, their opposition became violent.

Poor Muslims and those without powerful friends suffered the most. One of them was Bilal, an Abyssinian slave and one of the first believers in Islam. His master, Umayya, often took him out in the hot midday sun. He put a heavy rock on Bilal’s chest and ordered him to give up his religion.

The leaders of Mecca went further. Between 617 and 620, they began a social and economic boycott against Muslims and those who helped them. During this hard time, the Prophet (pbuh), Khadija, and Abu Talib spent their money to support the Muslims.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:mecca-mecca-7th-century
__historical_entity__:mecca-umayya-ibn-khalaf
Made fun of someone or something in an unkind way.
Said that idol worship was wrong.
Using physical force or cruelty.
From Abyssinia, the historical region associated with Ethiopia.
An organized refusal to trade or deal with a group as pressure.

hotspots.title: Bilal
hotspots.description: Bilal, an Abyssinian slave and early Muslim, suffered severe pressure because of his faith.

hotspots.title: Boycott
hotspots.description: Between 617 and 620, a social and economic boycott was used against Muslims and their supporters.

exercises.title: Step by Step
exercises.instructions: Put the events from Chapter 13 in the right order.
exercises.question: How did the opposition to Islam grow step by step?

sequencingItems.text: The leaders laughed whenever the Prophet (pbuh) walked by.
The Qur’an criticized the idols and warned against false worship.
Umayya ordered Bilal to give up his religion.
The leaders began a social and economic boycott against Muslims.

exercises.explanation: “At first, the leaders of Mecca only mocked Islam.” “But when the Qur’an criticized the idols and warned against false worship, their opposition became violent,” and poor Muslims such as Bilal suffered the most. Then “the leaders of Mecca went further”: between 617 and 620 they began a boycott.

feedback.correct: Well done. The opposition grew from mocking, to violence against weak Muslims, to a boycott.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the step words in Chapter 13: “At first …”, “But when …”, and “The leaders of Mecca went further.”

languageFocusExercises.title: From Mocking to Boycott
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the sentences in order. “At first”, “But when” and “went further” help.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the chapter show opposition becoming more and more serious?

sequencingItems.text: The leaders of Mecca went further.
At first, the leaders of Mecca only mocked Islam.
Between 617 and 620, they began a social and economic boycott against Muslims and those who helped them.
But when the Qur’an criticized the idols and warned against false worship, their opposition became violent.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “At first” sets the earliest stage, and “only” shows it was limited to mockery. “But when …” marks a change caused by a new event. “Went further” tells the reader that the next action will be even stronger, and the boycott sentence gives that action. These markers show escalation: Each step is more serious than the one before.

feedback.correct: Correct. You followed the opposition from mocking to violence to a boycott.
feedback.incorrect: Start with “At first”. “Went further” must come just before the stronger action it introduces.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong word or phrase, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you correct a repeated past action, a reported order and a purpose phrase?

errorItems.sentence: Whenever Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) walked by, they laugh and said that he was talking about messages from heaven.
He put a heavy rock on Bilal’s chest and ordered him give up his religion.
During this hard time, the Prophet (pbuh), Khadija, and Abu Talib spent their money for support the Muslims.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Whenever + past simple, past simple” describes a reaction that happened every time: Both verbs are in the past (“walked … laughed”). “Order + person + to + verb” reports a command. “To + verb” gives the purpose of an action: Why did they spend their money? To support the Muslims.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the repeated action, the reported order and the purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Check the tense after “whenever”, the word after “ordered him”, and the word before “support”. Then compare with Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Are “Those Without Powerful Friends”?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 13. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Poor Muslims and those without powerful friends suffered the most.” Who does “those without powerful friends” describe?
options: people who had no friends at all
people who had no strong supporters to protect them
powerful people who lost their friends
people who left their friends to become Muslims
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Those + without + noun” describes a group by what they did not have. This links back to Chapter 8: in Meccan society, protection came from strong people and tribes. The next sentence gives one clear example of such a person: Bilal, “an Abyssinian slave”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The phrase describes people who had no one strong to protect them.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word “powerful”. The phrase is not about having friends in general. Who is the example in the next sentence?

languageFocusExercises.title: Describe a Situation That Becomes More Serious
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say six sentences about a problem that got worse.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did the problem start, and how did it get worse?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should use “at first”, a change with “but when”, a repeated-past pattern with “whenever” or “often”, a reported command with “ordered/told + person + to + verb”, a group description with “those without...”, and a purpose phrase with “to + verb”.

feedback.correct: Keep the six sentences connected so the reader can follow the change, repeated behavior, command, vulnerability and purpose.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Set the earlier stage with “At first...”.
discussionPrompts.example: At first, some students only laughed at the new boy in our class.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Show a change with “But when...”.
discussionPrompts.example: But when he won the school prize, their behavior became worse.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Add repeated past behavior with “whenever” or “often”.
discussionPrompts.example: Whenever he walked into the classroom, they made jokes about his accent.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Report an order with “ordered/told + person + to + verb”.
discussionPrompts.example: Finally, the teacher told the students to stop and say sorry.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — Describe a group with “those without...”.
discussionPrompts.example: Those without friends in a new school often feel very lonely.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 6 — Explain an action’s purpose with “to + verb”.
discussionPrompts.example: The teacher also started a buddy plan to help new students feel welcome.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: When did the boycott against the Muslims begin?
beforeYouRead.quote: Between 617 and 620, they began a social and economic boycott

iCan: I can tell how the opposition to Islam grew step by step.
I can say what happened at first and what changed later.
I can describe a situation that slowly got worse.

pages.title: Boycott and Pressure
pages.content:
During the boycott, people had no food. Some died of hunger, and others even ate tree leaves to survive. The cries of hungry children could be heard everywhere.

Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) continued to ask people to stop worshipping idols and worship Allah alone. However, the leaders were proud of their old beliefs and did not want to change. The idols brought them money, trade, and power. Losing the idols meant losing wealth and influence, so they became hostile to Islam.

They also did not want to accept that people would be judged after death. They did not want to think about punishment for hurting people, making money unfairly, drinking alcohol, or doing other evil things. Tribal loyalty was another challenge because people feared losing their tribe’s protection.

vocabulary.definition: To stay alive in a difficult or dangerous situation.
A large amount of money or valuable possessions.
Unfriendly and strongly opposed to someone or something.
A penalty or consequence for wrongdoing.
Strong support for one’s tribe.

hotspots.title: Hunger
hotspots.description: During the boycott, hunger became so severe that some people ate tree leaves to survive.

hotspots.title: Fear of Change
hotspots.description: Leaders feared losing wealth, influence, and tribal protection if the old order changed.

exercises.title: What the Leaders Feared
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 14.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 14, what did the Quraysh leaders fear to lose if they left the idols?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 14 says: “The idols brought them money, trade, and power. Losing the idols meant losing wealth and influence, so they became hostile to Islam.”

feedback.correct: Right. The idols brought the leaders money and power, so they did not want to lose them.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 14 and find the words “Losing the idols meant …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Why Not Say Who Heard?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 14. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The cries of hungry children could be heard everywhere.” Why does the writer not say who heard the cries?
options: Because nobody really heard the cries; the writer imagines them to make the story sad.
Because only the leaders of Mecca heard them, and the writer does not want to name these leaders.
Because the cries are the important thing: Anyone in the area could hear them, so the listener does not matter.
Because the children heard their own cries, and nobody else was near them at that time.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Could be heard” is a passive form with “could”. The passive puts the cries at the start of the sentence and leaves out the listener because the listener could be anyone. With “everywhere”, it shows how widespread the hunger was.

feedback.correct: Correct. The passive keeps the focus on the cries and how widely they could be heard.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word “everywhere”. If the cries could be heard everywhere, who could hear them?

languageFocusExercises.title: Result or Reason?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence so that it keeps the same meaning. Use the start that is given.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you change “so” into “because”, and “because” into “so”?

transformItems.source: Losing the idols meant losing wealth and influence, so they became hostile to Islam.
transformItems.frame: They became hostile to Islam [blank] wealth and influence.
answers: because losing the idols meant losing
as losing the idols meant losing
since losing the idols meant losing
because losing their idols meant losing

transformItems.source: Tribal loyalty was another challenge because people feared losing their tribe’s protection.
transformItems.frame: People feared losing their tribe’s protection, [blank] another challenge.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So” introduces a result; “because” introduces a reason. When you change the order of the ideas, you change the linker but keep the same cause and effect. Notice the -ing forms after “meant” and “feared”: “meant losing”, “feared losing”. They name the loss the leaders and people were afraid of.

feedback.correct: Well done. You kept the same cause and effect in a new order.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: start the gap with “because” and keep “losing … meant losing”. Item 2: start the gap with “so”. Check the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 14.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong word or phrase, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the verbs after “stop” and “want”?

errorItems.sentence: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) continued to ask people to stop worship idols and worship Allah alone.
However, the leaders were proud of their old beliefs and did not want changing.
They did not want to think about punishment for hurting people, making money unfairly, drink alcohol, or doing other evil things.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Stop + -ing” means “no longer do something”; “stop to + verb” would mean stopping in order to do it. “Want + to + verb” expresses wish or unwillingness: “did not want to change”. After “for”, the list uses -ing forms, and every item must have the same form: “hurting …, making …, drinking …, or doing …”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the verb patterns and the parallel list.
feedback.incorrect: Check what follows “stop”, “want” and “for” in the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 14.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain Why People Resist Change
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about people who did not want to change.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did people refuse to change, and why?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should include a purpose phrase with “to + verb”, one continuation pattern with “continued to...”, one unwillingness pattern with “did not want to...”, one cause-result link with “so”, and one reason with “because”.

feedback.correct: Keep the ideas connected so the reader can follow the situation, persistence, resistance, feared consequence and reason.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Describe a difficult situation and one action done for a purpose.
discussionPrompts.example: Last winter, our town had no buses for two weeks, and some workers walked for hours to reach their jobs.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what someone continued to do.
discussionPrompts.example: The town council continued to ask people to share cars.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say what another person or group did not want to change.
discussionPrompts.example: However, many drivers did not want to change their habits.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Explain a feared consequence and its result with “so”.
discussionPrompts.example: They were afraid that sharing would make them late, so they kept driving alone.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5–6 — Give the reason with “because” and add one short list of related actions if natural.
discussionPrompts.example: They also said no because they did not know their neighbors. Sharing meant waiting, planning and talking to strangers.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. What happened to people during the boycott?
options: They moved to a new city.
beforeYouRead.quote: During the boycott, people had no food.

iCan: I can describe the boycott and why the leaders did not want to change.
I can give a result with “so” and a reason with “because”.
I can explain why people sometimes say no to a good change.

pages.title: Islam and Justice
pages.content:
In old Arab society, tribal loyalty was so strong that freedom of choice was difficult. If someone left the tribe’s way, that person could lose protection. It was almost like being stateless today. The leaders of Mecca tried to prevent members of their tribes from becoming Muslim.

The Quraysh leaders said Islam was breaking up families and destroying unity. In reality, Islam was calling people to a better form of unity based on justice, mercy, and belief in one Allah.

Before Islam, Mecca was a difficult place with much unfairness. Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) told people to be fair, to show respect to others, and to show mercy. In Islam, every person is important. Background, wealth, gender, and social power do not make one person more valuable than another. Jahiliyyah means a society without justice and mercy; Islam is the opposite because it brings peace and fairness.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:mecca-mecca-7th-century
__historical_entity__:mecca-quraysh
Without the protection or recognized belonging of a state or community.
The ability to make a choice without being forced.
To stop something from happening.
Kindness and compassion shown to others.
Justice and equal treatment.

hotspots.title: Freedom of Choice
hotspots.description: Strong tribal loyalty made freedom of choice difficult for people who wanted to change their beliefs.

hotspots.title: Unity and Justice
hotspots.description: Islam called people to unity based on justice, mercy, and belief in one Allah.

exercises.title: A Better Unity
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 15.
exercises.question: The Quraysh leaders said Islam was breaking up families and destroying unity. How does the writer answer this claim?
options: The writer agrees that tribal loyalty was the best way to keep families safe and united.
The writer says Islam was calling people to a better form of unity based on justice, mercy and belief in one Allah.
The writer says Islam asked people to build a new and stronger unity based on wealth, tribe and family name.
exercises.explanation: After the leaders’ claim, the writer says: “In reality, Islam was calling people to a better form of unity based on justice, mercy, and belief in one Allah.” The words “In reality” show that the writer does not accept the leaders’ claim.

feedback.correct: Correct. With “In reality”, the writer answers the claim: Islam offered unity based on justice, mercy and faith.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 15. Find the words “In reality” and see what comes after them.

languageFocusExercises.title: Their Claim or the Writer’s View?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it what the Quraysh leaders said, or the writer’s view? Sort the parts.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the chapter keep a reported claim separate from the writer’s own view?

items: Islam was calling people to a better form of unity …
In Islam, every person is important.
Before Islam, Mecca was a difficult place with much unfairness.

The writer’s own view: Islam was calling people to a better form of unity …
In Islam, every person is important.
Before Islam, Mecca was a difficult place with much unfairness.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “The Quraysh leaders said …” reports a claim; the writer does not present it as true. The next sentence starts with a contrast marker and gives the writer’s own view of Islam. Sentences without a reporting verb, such as “In Islam, every person is important”, are the writer’s own statements.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated the leaders’ claim from the writer’s view.
feedback.incorrect: Find the reporting verb “said” in the second paragraph of Chapter 15. Only the words after it belong to the leaders.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong word or phrase, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you correct “so … that”, “prevent … from” and “told … to”?

errorItems.sentence: In old Arab society, tribal loyalty was such strong that freedom of choice was difficult.
The leaders of Mecca tried to prevent members of their tribes to become Muslim.
Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) told people be fair, to show respect to others, and to show mercy.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So + adjective + that” links a strong degree to its result: Loyalty was so strong that free choice was difficult (“such” is used before a noun: “such strong loyalty”). “Prevent + person + from + -ing” means “stop someone doing something”. “Tell + person + to + verb” reports advice or an instruction.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the degree-result pattern, the prevention pattern and the reported instruction.
feedback.incorrect: Check what comes before an adjective + “that”, what follows “prevent … ”, and what follows “told people”. Then compare with Chapter 15.

languageFocusExercises.title: Pressure, Reality and Value
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 15 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases tell us about tribal pressure and the value of every person?

matchingPairs.right: the group might no longer keep them safe
nearly the same as having no country to belong to now
What was actually true was different:

matchingPairs.left: based on justice, mercy, and belief in one Allah
matchingPairs.right: with these values as its foundation

matchingPairs.left: do not make one person more valuable than another
matchingPairs.right: do not give anyone greater worth

correctAnswer.that person could lose protection: the group might no longer keep them safe
correctAnswer.almost like being stateless today: nearly the same as having no country to belong to now
correctAnswer.In reality: What was actually true was different:
correctAnswer.based on justice, mercy, and belief in o: with these values as its foundation
correctAnswer.do not make one person more valuable tha: do not give anyone greater worth

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Could” shows a possible result, not a certain one. “Almost like” makes a careful comparison with today. “In reality” introduces what the writer sees as true, in contrast to a claim. “Based on” names the foundation of something. “Make + person + comparative adjective” in the negative rejects the idea that background or wealth gives more value.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each phrase with its meaning in the chapter.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 15 again. Replace each phrase with your answer and check that the sentence still makes sense.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain Pressure and a Fairer Alternative
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five or six sentences about strong pressure on people, and a fairer way.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was the pressure, and what is a fairer way?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response should naturally use one “so ... that” relationship, one “if ... could ...” consequence, one prevention phrase, one reported claim, one contrast marker such as “In reality” or “however”, and one sentence explaining what a fair system is based on.

feedback.correct: Keep the response connected so the reader can follow the pressure, consequence, reported claim, contrast and alternative principle.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Describe a pressure that was so strong that it affected people’s choices.
discussionPrompts.example: In our class, the pressure to wear expensive shoes was so strong that some students felt ashamed of their old ones.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Explain what could happen if someone resisted that pressure.
discussionPrompts.example: If someone wore cheap shoes, other students might laugh at them.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say how a person or group tried to prevent a change.
discussionPrompts.example: A few popular students tried to stop the school from making a simple uniform rule.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Report what that group said or believed.
discussionPrompts.example: They said that a simple uniform would make everyone look boring.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5–6 — Contrast the claim with another view and explain what the fairer alternative is based on.
discussionPrompts.example: In reality, a simple uniform helps students feel equal. A fairer school is based on respect, not on what people can buy.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What did the Prophet (pbuh) tell people to be?
options: to be rich, strong and proud
to be fair, to show respect and to show mercy
to be quiet, busy and careful
beforeYouRead.quote: Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) told people to be fair, to show respect to others, and to show mercy.

iCan: I can explain how Islam called people to justice and mercy.
I can tell the difference between what people said and what was true.
I can suggest a fairer way to treat people in my class or town.

groupTask.title: Then and Now: A Fairer Community

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You copy one sentence from the book exactly that shows the problem or the fairer way.

roles.name: Explainer
roles.job: You explain the sentence in your own words in two or three sentences.

roles.name: Today Researcher
roles.job: You describe how people or institutions try to solve a similar problem today.

roles.name: Designer and Presenter
roles.job: You put everything on a one-page poster, or record a two-minute audio report, and present it.

steps: Choose one problem the book describes: weak protection, usury and debt, tribal pressure, or the unequal treatment of women and slaves.
Copy one sentence from the book exactly, for example: “Powerful people controlled many parts of life, while poor and weak people lived in misery.” or “In Islam, every person is important.”
Explain the sentence in your own words, then describe how people or institutions try to solve a similar problem today, for example a school fund, a fair loan or a club rule.
Use at least three patterns from the Language Focus, such as “because of …”, “while …”, “prevent … from …” or “so … that …”. Nobody speaks as a person from the story; you only quote and explain.
groupTask.share: Each group presents its poster or plays its audio report, reads the quote from the book aloud and names one fair idea for their own school or town.
groupTask.solo: Choose one problem, copy one sentence from the book, explain it in two sentences and write two sentences about how people solve a similar problem today.

places.name: Mecca
places.text: Mecca is the holy city of Islam, and the Holy Ka’ba is here. The Qur’an describes Mecca as a valley where no crops grow, so people made money through trade. In the 5th century, the Quraysh tribe took over the city and the Ka’ba. In the pilgrimage season, people went to big fairs such as Ukaz, Majannah and Dhul-Majaz first, and then to Arafat.
places.teacherNote: The book does not give the locations of Arafat or of the fairs (Ukaz, Majannah, Dhul-Majaz), so they are not drawn. Chapter 2 adds that the Qiblah is in Mecca and that Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) was born here and spent 52 years of his life here.
places.question: Why did the people of Mecca make money through trade?

places.name: Yemen
places.text: After the discovery of Zamzam water, the Jurhumites from Yemen settled in Mecca. Ishmael (pbuh) learned Arabic from them. Later, Meccan merchants traveled safely to Yemen to trade.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say which way the Jurhumites traveled, so both lines are only a guide. Chapter 4 says the Khuza’a tribe later defeated the Jurhum tribe, but it does not say where the Khuza’a came from, so they are not on the map.
places.question: What did Ishmael (pbuh) learn from the Jurhumites?

places.name: Palestine
places.text: Prophet Abraham (pbuh) came to Mecca to build the Holy Ka’ba again with his son Ishmael (pbuh). After he completed his mission and invited people for pilgrimage, he returned to Palestine.
places.teacherNote: The book gives no date for Abraham (pbuh) and does not say where he set out from when he first brought Hagar and Ishmael (pbuh) to Mecca. Only his return to Palestine (chapter 4) is drawn.
places.question: What did Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh) do together in Mecca?

places.name: Iraq
places.text: Iraq was one of the places where Meccan merchants traded. Hashim ibn Abd Manaf and the Quraysh leaders made special trade agreements, so the merchants could travel there safely.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 5 names Iraq only as a trade destination. The circle and the route are approximate.
places.question: Who was Hashim ibn Abd Manaf, and how did he help Mecca?

places.name: Ethiopia
places.text: Ethiopia was another place where Meccan merchants traded. Thanks to the trade agreements of the Quraysh, they could travel there safely.
places.teacherNote: B1 does not say whether the merchants reached Ethiopia by land or by sea, so no route is drawn; Ethiopia is joined to Mecca only by a thread in the chapter 5 step. In chapter 13 the book calls Bilal “an Abyssinian slave”.
places.question: Which four places does chapter 5 name for Meccan trade?

places.name: Byzantium
places.text: When Islam began, the Byzantine Empire was a powerful state. It traded with both the north and the south of Arabia. Meccan merchants also traded in Byzantium.
places.teacherNote: The soft area only shows that the Byzantine lands lay to the north. B1 does not describe their borders; the B2 book tells more about this empire.
places.question: Which two powerful empires does chapter 4 name?

places.name: Sassanid Empire
places.text: The Sassanid Empire was the other powerful state when Islam began. Like the Byzantine Empire, it traded with both the north and the south of Arabia.
places.teacherNote: B1 does not say where the Sassanid lands were. The area east of Iraq is only approximate; the B2 book says the Sassanids were the Arabs’ neighbors in the east.
places.question: Why were these two empires important for trade in Arabia?

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your understanding of the whole story through eight evidence-based questions.

exercises.title: The Republic of Merchants
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 1.
exercises.question: Before Islam, Mecca was known as the “Republic of Merchants.” What does this name tell us about the city?
options: A central government controlled trade across all of Arabia.
A council of rich merchants led the city, so wealth meant power.
Poor and weak people had a strong voice in city decisions.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “Before Islam, Mecca was led by a council of rich merchants. For this reason, the city was known as the Republic of Merchants.” The same paragraph adds: “Powerful people controlled many parts of life, while poor and weak people lived in misery.”

feedback.correct: Well done. The name shows that money and leadership went together: The richest merchants ran the city, while the poor had little say.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 1. Who led Mecca, and what happened to poor and weak people? Remember that Arabia had no central government.

exercises.title: A Religion Forgotten
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Connect Chapters 3 and 4.
exercises.question: How did religious life in Mecca change after the Khuza’a took control of the city?
options: People stopped visiting the Ka’ba and moved to other cities.
The Jurhumites came back and taught Abraham’s religion again.
People forgot the religion of Abraham (pbuh) and worshipped idols.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “Arabs accepted the religion of Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh), so the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site.” Chapter 4: “Under Khuza’a rule, people forgot the religion of Abraham (pbuh) and started worshipping many idols.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Mecca began with the religion of Abraham (pbuh), but under Khuza’a rule people forgot it and idol worship spread.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Compare the end of Chapter 3 with the second paragraph of Chapter 4. What happened to the religion of Abraham (pbuh)?

exercises.title: Who Should Lead?
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Some rich leaders asked why Muhammad (pbuh) should be the leader while they were rich and important. What does their question show?
options: They believed wealth and status should decide who leads.
They wanted the Prophet (pbuh) to share his wealth with them.
They thought the poor should choose the leader of Mecca.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 explains their way of thinking: “For the wealthy Quraysh, money and tribe were the most important values.” So they judged a leader by his wealth and position, not by his message.

feedback.correct: Well done. The leaders measured a person by money and status, so they could not accept a leader who was not one of the rich.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 7. What were the most important values for the wealthy Quraysh?

exercises.title: Why Sons Mattered
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 8, families wanted many sons mainly so that the sons could run the family business.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “Men were often seen as valuable because they were fighters in wars. To earn respect from other tribes, families wanted to have many sons.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. Sons mattered because they could fight, and many fighters brought a family respect from other tribes.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at the first paragraph of Chapter 8. Why were men seen as valuable, and what did families want to earn?

exercises.title: Poets as Media
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 9.
exercises.question: Why does the writer say poets were “like the media of the people”?
options: Poets carried news of prices from one trade fair to another.
Poetry kept tribal history alive and praised or criticized tribes.
Poets wrote the rules that every tribe had to follow.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “Poetry kept tribal history alive, praised tribes, and criticized enemies. In those days, poets were like the media of the people.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Like the media today, poetry told people what to remember, whom to praise and whom to criticize.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Reread the last paragraph of Chapter 9. What did poetry do for the tribes?

exercises.title: Belief in Mecca
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: Before Islam, not every person in Mecca worshipped idols.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10: “In Mecca, most people also worshipped idols.” But: “Some people, called Hanifs, followed the old religion of Abraham (pbuh).”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The word “most” is important: most people worshipped idols, but the Hanifs followed the religion of Abraham (pbuh).
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 10 carefully. Does it say “all” or “most”? Who were the Hanifs?

exercises.title: Fear of Judgement
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 14.
exercises.question: Why did the Quraysh leaders refuse to accept that people would be judged after death?
options: They believed their idols would protect them on that day.
They thought only poor people would be judged for their actions.
They did not want to think about punishment for their wrongdoing.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 14: “They did not want to think about punishment for hurting people, making money unfairly, drinking alcohol, or doing other evil things.”

feedback.correct: Well done. Accepting judgement after death meant accepting that their unfair actions would be punished.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the last paragraph of Chapter 14. What did the leaders not want to think about?

exercises.title: Freedom of Choice
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: It was hard for a person to choose a new religion because leaving the tribe’s way could mean losing its protection.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 15: “In old Arab society, tribal loyalty was so strong that freedom of choice was difficult. If someone left the tribe’s way, that person could lose protection. It was almost like being stateless today.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. Without the tribe, a person had no protection, so choosing Islam was a real risk.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 15. What could happen to someone who left the tribe’s way?

pages.content: Review and use grammar, meaning relationships and communicative language from across the book.

exercises.title: Notice: Once, or Again and Again?
exercises.instructions: Did it happen once, or again and again? Put each sentence in its group.
exercises.question: Which words show that an action happened again and again?

items: This era ended when the first revelation of the Qur’an began in 610 CE.
Later, in the 5th century, the Quraysh tribe took over the city and the Ka’ba.
In 610, Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) started teaching Islam in Mecca.
In these months, people focused on worship, showed respect, and stayed away from fighting.
Powerful people were usually merchants who lent money with usury.
Whenever Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) walked by, they laughed …
His master, Umayya, often took him out in the hot midday sun.

Happened once: This era ended when the first revelation of the Qur’an began in 610 CE.
Later, in the 5th century, the Quraysh tribe took over the city and the Ka’ba.
In 610, Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) started teaching Islam in Mecca.
Happened again and again: In these months, people focused on worship, showed respect, and stayed away from fighting.
Powerful people were usually merchants who lent money with usury.
Whenever Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) walked by, they laughed …
His master, Umayya, often took him out in the hot midday sun.

exercises.explanation: The past simple can describe one finished event or a past habit; the words around the verb tell us which. A date or a time marker (in 610, in the 5th century, later, when + one event) points to one event. Frequency words (usually, often), “whenever” (= every time that) and a repeated period (“In these months”, every year) show that the action happened again and again. The book uses both to tell history: Single turning points and the everyday life around them.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the time words to tell single events from repeated ones.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the time words in each sentence: a date or “later”, or words like usually, often, whenever and in these months?

exercises.title: Notice: Whose View Is It?
exercises.instructions: Read the four sentences from Chapters 7, 10, 12 and 15. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: In three of these sentences, the writer reports what a group in the story thought, felt or said. Which sentence is the writer’s own statement?
options: They thought these idols helped them talk to Allah.
The leaders of Quraysh felt that Islam was a danger to their power …
The Quraysh leaders said Islam was breaking up families and destroying unity.
Usury caused a big gap between social classes.
exercises.explanation: Verbs such as “thought”, “felt that” and “said” report the ideas of people in the story; they do not mean that the writer agrees. The idol worshippers thought the idols helped them, the leaders felt that Islam was a danger, and the leaders said it was destroying unity. “Usury caused a big gap between social classes” has no reporting verb: it is the writer’s own statement about cause and effect.

feedback.correct: Correct. A reporting verb tells you whose idea it is. Without one, the writer is speaking.
feedback.incorrect: Look for a reporting verb (thought, felt that, said). Which sentence does not have one?

exercises.title: Notice: Who Did It?
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from the book. Is the statement true or false?
exercises.question: “… people from poor backgrounds were often treated badly.” “… Zamzam water had not been discovered yet.” “Slaves lived in very cruel conditions and were bought and sold like animals.” “The cries of hungry children could be heard everywhere.” Statement: In these sentences, the poor people, the water, the slaves and the cries are the ones who did the actions of treating, discovering, buying and selling, and hearing.
exercises.explanation: These are passive forms: be + past participle (were treated, had been discovered, were bought and sold, could be heard). The subject is the person or thing that the action happens to, not the doer. The writer leaves the doer out because it is general, unknown or not important, and keeps the reader’s attention on the people who suffered, on the water, and on the cries.

feedback.correct: Correct. In a passive sentence the subject receives the action; the doer is left out.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Did the slaves buy and sell, or were they bought and sold by others? Did the cries hear, or were they heard?

exercises.title: Build: Link the Ideas
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentences from the book with words from the bank. Two are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word gives a result, a cause, a contrast or a surprise?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Arabs accepted the religion of Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh), [blank] the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site. … [blank] the rich lived in luxury with gold plates and silver cups, the poor struggled to survive. … Arab people in that period actually believed in one main God, Allah, as the Creator. [blank], they also worshipped many idols. … They were very rich, and other tribes respected them [blank] trade and the idols in the Ka’ba.
exercises.explanation: “So” introduces the result of the Arabs’ choice: First they accepted the religion, then the Ka’ba became a pilgrimage site (“because” would turn the order of cause and result round). “While” puts two groups side by side in one sentence: The rich and the poor. “However” starts a new sentence with something we would not expect after belief in one God, so “Therefore” does not fit. “Because of” + a noun phrase (trade and the idols) gives the cause; “because” would need a subject and a verb.

feedback.correct: Well done. You chose each linker by its meaning and by what follows it.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask two questions: Is it a result, a cause or a contrast? And does a noun phrase or a full clause (subject + verb) come next?

exercises.title: Build: What Follows the Verb?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapters 5, 12 and 14.
exercises.question: After “allowed merchants”, “stop Islam” and “feared”, which form comes next?

formChoices.sentence: These agreements allowed merchants [choice] safely and trade in places like Byzantium, Yemen, Iraq, and Ethiopia.
Meccan leaders tried to stop Islam [choice].
Tribal loyalty was another challenge because people feared [choice] their tribe’s protection.

exercises.explanation: Each verb has its own pattern. “Allow + person + to + verb” gives permission or a chance: the agreements allowed merchants to travel. “Stop + person/thing + from + -ing” means not letting something happen: The leaders tried to stop Islam from growing. “Fear + -ing” names the thing people were afraid of: They feared losing their tribe’s protection.

feedback.correct: Correct. Allow … to + verb, stop … from + -ing, fear + -ing.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb before the gap. Check Chapter 5 (the agreements), Chapter 12 (the last sentence) and Chapter 14 (the last sentence).

exercises.title: Build: Fix One Mistake
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct form.
exercises.question: Can you fix a question and two verb forms?

errorItems.sentence: When Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) started calling people to Islam, some rich leaders asked why should Muhammad be the leader while they were rich and important.
Men were often saw as valuable because they were fighters in wars.
They also did not want to accept that people would judge after death.

exercises.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order: asked why + subject + verb (“asked why Muhammad should be the leader”), not question order. The passive needs be + past participle: “were often seen as valuable”. People do not judge here; they are the ones who are judged, so the sentence needs the passive “would be judged”. “Would” shows a future event seen from the past.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the word order and the two passives.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with the book: Chapter 7 (the rich leaders’ question), Chapter 8 (men and wars) and Chapter 14 (what happens after death).

exercises.question: Can you join two sentences with “while” and start with a new subject?

transformItems.source: Rich women, like Khadija, could run their own businesses. … many poor women had no rights and faced unfair treatment.
transformItems.frame: While [blank], many poor women had no rights and faced unfair treatment.
answers: rich women, like Khadija, could run their own businesses
rich women like Khadija could run their own businesses
rich women could run their own businesses
rich women, like Khadija, were able to run their own businesses
rich women were able to run their own businesses
rich women, like Khadija, could run their businesses

transformItems.source: Later, the Khuza’a tribe came to Mecca, defeated the Jurhum tribe, and took control of the city.
transformItems.frame: Later, the Jurhum tribe [blank] by the Khuza’a tribe, and the Khuza’a took control of the city.

exercises.explanation: “While” joins two different situations in one sentence, so no second linker is needed. The “while” clause comes first and is followed by a comma. In the second sentence, the passive (“was defeated”) puts the Jurhum tribe, the group that lost, at the start; “by” names the winner.

feedback.correct: Well done. You joined a contrast with “while” and used the passive to change the focus.
feedback.incorrect: For the first frame, write what rich women could do. For the second, use was + past participle because the Jurhum tribe did not defeat anyone.

exercises.title: Use: Our School Garden
exercises.instructions: This text is new. Complete it with words from the bank. Two are not needed.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words to tell a school story?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last year, the land behind our school was full of rubbish. Some parents thought that a garden would be a waste of time. [blank], our class decided to try. The rubbish [blank] by students and teachers in two days, and the head teacher allowed us to grow vegetables there. [blank] the spring rain, the plants grew very fast. Everyone loves the garden now, [blank] nobody leaves rubbish there any more.
exercises.explanation: “Some parents thought that …” reports a view, and “However” introduces a different reaction. “Was collected by …” is passive: The rubbish did not collect anything, students and teachers collected it. “Because of” + noun (the spring rain) gives a cause, and “so” gives the result. The text also uses “allowed us to grow”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language to describe a change in a new place.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Is it a contrast, a cause or a result? Who did the collecting? Does a noun or a subject + verb come next?

exercises.title: Use: Check a Class Report
exercises.instructions: A student wrote these sentences. Each has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correction.
exercises.question: Can you fix the mistakes in a student’s report?

errorItems.sentence: Our teacher asked us why were we late for the museum trip.
A new rule stops students from to run in the corridors.
The trip was plan by the student council.

exercises.explanation: Reported question: asked why + subject + verb (“why we were late”). Stop + person + from + -ing (“stops students from running”). Passive: was + past participle (“was planned by the student council”).

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s patterns to correct new sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Check the three patterns: asked why + statement order; stop … from + -ing; was + past participle.

exercises.title: Use: A Change in My Community
exercises.instructions: Write five or six sentences about a change at school or in your town.
exercises.question: What changed, and what did people think about it?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Last year, a new bus stop was built near our school because many students walked a long way in the rain. At first, some shopkeepers thought that the buses would make the street too busy. They asked why the stop could not be further away. However, the town kept the stop, and the street was made safer with a new crossing. This allowed younger students to arrive on time and stopped them from waiting in the rain. That is why most families are happy with the change now.”

feedback.correct: Check your sentences: because / because of; so / That is why; However / While; thought that / asked why + statement order; a passive (was + past participle); allow … to / stop … from + -ing.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 1–2 — The change and the reason: “Last year, … was built/opened/changed … because / because of …”
discussionPrompts.example: Last year, a new bike lane was built on our main street. It was built because of the heavy traffic near the school.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — One group’s view: “Some people thought/felt that …” or “They asked why … (subject + verb)”
discussionPrompts.example: Some shop owners thought that the lane would keep customers away.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — A different view or fact: “However, …” or “While some …, others …”
discussionPrompts.example: However, many parents were happy because their children could ride to school safely.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — The result: “This allowed … to … / stopped … from …ing, so … . That is why …”
discussionPrompts.example: This allowed more students to cycle every day and stopped many cars from driving near the school, so the street became quieter. That is why most people like the lane now.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Demonstrate whole-book B1 understanding through ten varied tasks.

exercises.title: No Central Government
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 1 with one word: tribes, cities or kings.
exercises.question: What was the basis of society in Arabia before Islam?
exercises.fillBlanksText: There was no central government in Arabia, and [blank] were the basis of society.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “Life was hard and chaotic. There was no central government in Arabia, and tribes were the basis of society.”

feedback.correct: Yes. With no state to protect people, the tribe took its place, as Chapter 8 later shows.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 1. What took the place of a government?

exercises.title: The Holy City
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason the story gives.
exercises.question: Why is Mecca the holy city of Islam?
options: It was the richest trading center in Arabia.
Allah chose it as the location of His House, the Ka’ba.
The Quraysh tribe had ruled it since the 5th century.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2 says: “Mecca is the holy city of Islam. Allah chose this city to be the location of His House, the Holy Ka’ba.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Mecca’s holiness comes from Allah’s choice, not from its trade or its rulers.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle paragraph of Chapter 2. What did Allah choose Mecca for?

exercises.title: Key Words
exercises.instructions: Match each word with its meaning in the story.
exercises.question: What does each word mean in the story?

matchingPairs.right: the direction Muslims face during salah
the water whose discovery brought people to settle in Mecca
a big trade fair held in the pilgrimage season
people who followed the old religion of Abraham (pbuh)

correctAnswer.Qiblah: the direction Muslims face during salah
correctAnswer.Zamzam: the water whose discovery brought people to settle in Mecca
correctAnswer.Ukaz: a big trade fair held in the pilgrimage season
correctAnswer.Hanifs: people who followed the old religion of Abraham (pbuh)

exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “The Qiblah, the direction Muslims face during salah, is also located in Mecca.” Chapter 3: “After the discovery of Zamzam water, the Jurhumites from Yemen settled in Mecca.” Chapter 6: “Big trade fairs such as Ukaz, Majannah, and Dhul-Majaz took place during this time.” Chapter 10: “Some people, called Hanifs, followed the old religion of Abraham (pbuh).”

feedback.correct: Yes. Each word is linked to Mecca’s religious or trading life.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 2, 3, 6 and 10.

exercises.title: Hashim’s Agreements
exercises.instructions: Choose the best explanation.
exercises.question: How did Hashim ibn Abd Manaf help Mecca’s economy grow?
options: He opened new farms in the dry valley around Mecca.
He stopped the fighting between the Khuza’a and the Jurhum.
His trade agreements let merchants travel and trade safely abroad.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5 says: “He and the Quraysh leaders made special trade agreements with other tribes and nations. These agreements allowed merchants to travel safely and trade in places like Byzantium, Yemen, Iraq, and Ethiopia.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Safe travel meant more trade, and more trade made Mecca wealthy.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 5. What did the agreements allow merchants to do?

exercises.title: Causes and Results
exercises.instructions: Match each cause with its result in the story.
exercises.question: What did each of these lead to?

matchingPairs.left: Mecca’s place on the trade routes
matchingPairs.right: The city became busy and wealthy.
The rich became richer and the poor poorer.
People fell deeper into debt.
Some Muslims died of hunger.

correctAnswer.Mecca’s place on the trade routes: The city became busy and wealthy.
correctAnswer.Lending money with usury: The rich became richer and the poor poorer.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Because Mecca was in the middle of important trade routes, it became a busy and wealthy city.” Chapter 6: “In the city, lending money with usury was widespread. This made the rich richer and the poor poorer.” Chapter 7: “these habits often pushed people deeper into debt.” Chapter 14: “During the boycott, people had no food. Some died of hunger”.

feedback.correct: Yes. You linked each cause with the result the story gives.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 5, 6, 7 and 14. Find the words “because”, “made” and “pushed”.

exercises.title: The Work of Slaves
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: In old Mecca, slaves usually did the easiest work, so owning slaves said little about a person’s wealth.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9 says: “Slaves lived in very cruel conditions and were bought and sold like animals. They did the most difficult work, and owning many slaves was a sign of wealth.”

feedback.correct: Right. Slaves did the hardest work, and owning many of them showed wealth.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 9. What work did slaves do?

exercises.title: Omens and Soothsayers
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: In the Age of Ignorance, people often asked soothsayers and checked omens before they made a decision.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10 says: “Life in the Age of Ignorance was also full of superstitions. People believed in kahins, or soothsayers, and checked omens before making decisions.”

feedback.correct: True. Superstition was part of the religious disorder of the time.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last two sentences of Chapter 10.

exercises.title: Hearing the Qur’an
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: How did the first Muslims respond when they heard the Prophet (pbuh) read the Qur’an?
options: They were sure it was from Allah, and it touched their hearts.
They laughed and said he talked about messages from heaven.
They asked the Quraysh leaders what they should believe.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 says: “When they heard Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) read the Qur’an, they were sure it was from Allah. This message changed them deeply. It touched their hearts and minds and made them feel great respect.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The same Qur’an that the leaders ignored changed these listeners deeply.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 11. The laughing came from the leaders in Chapter 13.

exercises.title: Help in Hard Times
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 13 with one word: money, houses or weapons.
exercises.question: How did the Prophet (pbuh), Khadija and Abu Talib help during the boycott?
exercises.fillBlanksText: During this hard time, the Prophet (pbuh), Khadija, and Abu Talib spent their [blank] to support the Muslims.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “Between 617 and 620, they began a social and economic boycott against Muslims and those who helped them. During this hard time, the Prophet (pbuh), Khadija, and Abu Talib spent their money to support the Muslims.”

feedback.correct: Yes. They used their own wealth to help the Muslims survive.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 13. What did they spend?

exercises.title: From Valley to Boycott
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: How does the history of Mecca unfold in the book?

sequencingItems.text: Hashim ibn Abd Manaf makes trade agreements with other nations.
Ishmael (pbuh) learns Arabic from the Jurhumites.
The leaders of Mecca begin a boycott against the Muslims.
The Quraysh tribe takes over the city and the Ka’ba.
The first revelation of the Qur’an begins.

exercises.explanation: Ishmael and the Jurhumites (Chapter 3), the Quraysh in the 5th century (Chapter 4), Hashim’s trade agreements (Chapter 5), the first revelation in 610 (Chapters 2 and 11), and the boycott between 617 and 620 (Chapter 13).

feedback.correct: Yes. The book moves from the first settlers to the Quraysh, and then to the call to Islam and the pressure against it.
feedback.incorrect: Think about how Mecca grew: First settlers, then new rulers, then trade, and only then the call to Islam and the pressure against it.
